title: Reading the Range from a Graph
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Explain how the range of a function can be determined directly from its graph, and illustrate with a simple example.
finalAnswer: Project the graph onto the $y$-axis: the range is the set of all $y$-values covered, i.e. $\{y : (x, y) \text{ lies on the graph for some } x\}$.

steps.title: Swap the Direction of Attention
steps.explanation: Domain questions ask which vertical slices of the plane the graph occupies; range questions ask which horizontal slices it occupies. Scanning left-to-right gives the domain, scanning bottom-to-top gives the range.
steps.why: Framing both as projections makes the pair of ideas symmetric and easy to recall.

steps.title: Track Extremes and Gaps
steps.explanation: Find the lowest and highest points of the graph, watching carefully for holes, asymptotes, or jumps that punch gaps into the vertical coverage. For f(x) = x^2 the vertex at (0, 0) and upward opening give range [0, infinity); for f(x) = 1/x the graph never touches y = 0, so the range is all nonzero reals.
steps.why: Endpoints included versus excluded, and gaps between branches, are where range answers usually go wrong.

steps.title: Cross-Check Algebraically
steps.explanation: A quick sign or bound argument should agree with the picture. If the graph suggests range [0, 4] but a formula check shows values above 4 are possible, one of the two readings needs revising.
steps.why: Matching visual and algebraic evidence turns a guess into a verified answer.
